Number games with names were popular: a Pompeii graffito reads, in effect, 'I love her whose number is 545.' NERON KAISAR written in Hebrew letters (nrwn qsr) adds to 666 (50+200+6+50 + 100+60+200); the Latin form Nero Caesar (nrw qsr) gives 616, and 616 is the reading of some ancient witnesses, including P115 (P.Oxy. 4499, 3rd-4th century) and Codex Ephraemi; Irenaeus knew of 616 but defended 666. A Hebrew document from Murabba'at (Mur 18, dated to Nero's reign) spells Nero's name as nrwn qsr, supporting the spelling used (Hillers). Irenaeus himself (Against Heresies 5.30) proposed Euanthas, Lateinos and Teitan, all equalling 666, but counselled against dogmatism.

The number identifies the beast for those with 'wisdom'. Leading proposals: (1) Nero Caesar by Hebrew gematria, with the 616 variant seen as a scribe's adjustment to the Latin spelling, now the majority scholarly view but disputed (critics note that it requires a Hebrew transliteration in a Greek book, that Irenaeus did not mention Nero, and that the spelling of Caesar varies); (2) the Greek word for beast (therion) written in Hebrew letters also equals 666, so the number may simply mean 'beast' (Bauckham); (3) 666 is a triangular number (of 36, itself triangular of 8), linking to the beast as 'an eighth' (17:11) (Bauckham); (4) a symbolic number of falling short of seven three times over, 'a human number' (Greek arithmos anthropou can mean 'a human number' rather than 'one man's number'), the counterfeit of perfection; (5) a future individual whose name will compute to 666. Many scholars combine symbolic and historical readings.
Nero Caesar (nrwn qsr = 666; Latin spelling = 616), confirming the first-century referent; 'let the one who has insight calculate' implies the first readers could do so (Gentry, Chilton).
Also Nero, as part of the case that the whole prophecy was fulfilled before AD 70.

Lateinos ('the Latin one', Irenaeus' suggestion) taken as the Latin church or papacy; some Protestant historicists computed papal titles such as Vicarius Filii Dei in Roman numerals as 666, though whether that was an official papal title is disputed (Elliott, Barnes, Smith).

The name of the future Antichrist, which believers will be able to calculate when he appears; futurists generally warn against attaching it to present figures and often note the symbolic overtone of six as the number of man (Walvoord, Thomas).
A symbol of human and satanic imperfection, always falling short of God's seven, characterising every beastly power; some idealists accept Nero as the first-century example (Hendriksen, Beale).
Here is a call for wisdom: let the one who has insight calculate

Daniel 12:10 says the wise (maskilim) will understand the meaning of the end-time events while the wicked will not; Daniel 11:33-35 shows the wise teaching and suffering under persecution. Revelation 17:9 repeats the formula for the seven heads.

John invites careful discernment, not curiosity: the wise see through the beast's claims. Whether 'calculate' requires literal gematria or spiritual discernment of the beast's character is part of the 666 debate.

The sea beast is Rome, especially Nero (the sixth head, 17:10), whose 42-month persecution (64-68), death by the sword and the empire's near-collapse and revival in 68-69 fit the chapter; 666 is Nero Caesar by Hebrew gematria. The land beast is either the imperial cult's provincial priesthood in Asia or the Jewish leadership that sided with Rome against Christians (Gentry, The Beast of Revelation; Chilton). The chapter therefore describes events the first readers would face 'soon'.

Agrees that the beast is Nero and Rome and that the chapter was fulfilled by AD 70, as part of a system in which all prophecy, including the Second Coming and resurrection, was fulfilled then; critics note this departs from the historic creeds, while proponents argue that the time-statements require it.

The sea beast is papal Rome, which inherited the western empire's power; its 42 months are 1,260 years of supremacy; the healed wound is the revival of Roman power through the papacy; the land beast is the papal clergy (Barnes, Elliott) or, in Seventh-day Adventist teaching, the United States enforcing religious law (Uriah Smith); 666 has been computed from Lateinos or papal titles. This was the dominant Protestant reading from the Reformation into the nineteenth century.

The sea beast is the future Antichrist, a world ruler over a revived Roman or global empire during the last 3.5 years of Daniel's seventieth week; the land beast is a personal false prophet; the image may stand in a rebuilt temple and the mark will be a literal requirement for commerce; the number will identify the Antichrist when he appears (Walvoord, Thomas).

The two beasts are recurring realities throughout the church age: coercive political power that demands absolute loyalty, and the religious, cultural or ideological propaganda that serves it. Rome was the first readers' example; every age has its own, culminating at the end (Hendriksen, Milligan).

Many recent commentators (Beale, Osborne, Ladd, Bauckham, Keener) hold that John addressed Roman imperial power and probably drew on the Nero legend, while seeing Rome as a type of a final antichristian power to come and of beastly power in every age; Ladd, a historic premillennialist, stresses a future personal Antichrist foreshadowed by Rome.
How does the beast imitate the Lamb (a slain-yet-living head, worship, a mark like God's seal, universal authority)? What does that suggest about how evil works?
Weigh the case for and against reading 666 as Nero Caesar. How much does the 616 variant help, and what are the strongest objections?
The second beast looks like a lamb but speaks like a dragon. Where might religious or cultural institutions today serve idolatrous power?
How does the economic dimension of the mark ('no one could buy or sell') change if it is read against first-century trade guilds, versus future technology?
Why does John interrupt the vision with 'a call for the perseverance and faith of the saints' (13:10), and how should the different views apply it?
The Lamb on Mount Zion, Three Angels, and the Harvest of the Earth

In answer to the beasts of chapter 13, John sees the Lamb standing on Mount Zion with the 144,000 who bear his and his Father's name, singing a new song as pure, truthful firstfruits who follow him wherever he goes. Three angels then fly in midheaven: one proclaims the eternal gospel and calls all nations to worship the Creator, one announces the fall of Babylon the great, and one warns that those who worship the beast and take its mark will drink the undiluted wine of God's wrath. A voice blesses those who die in the Lord. The chapter closes with two harvests: one like a son of man reaps the earth with a sickle, and an angel gathers the vine of the earth into the great winepress of God's wrath, from which blood flows for 1,600 stadia.
The Lamb and the 144,000 on Mount Zion
First angel: the eternal gospel and the call to fear God
Second angel: Babylon the great has fallen
Third angel: warning against the mark; the blessed dead
The grain harvest by one like a son of man
The vintage and the winepress of God's wrath

Chapter 14 completes the central triptych of chapters 12-14 by setting the Lamb and his people against the dragon and the beasts, and by previewing the end: Babylon's fall (chapters 17-18), the final judgment and the coming of the Son of Man (chapter 19). Its imagery comes from Israel's worship and harvest calendar. Mount Zion is the city of God's king (Psalm 2) and the place of deliverance (Joel 2:32); the 144,000 are pictured as both a holy army pure for battle (Deuteronomy 23; the Qumran War Scroll) and a firstfruits offering (Leviticus 23). The three angels echo the prophets' oracles against Babylon (Isaiah 21; Jeremiah 25 and 51), the cup of wrath, and the fire and smoke of Sodom and Edom (Genesis 19; Isaiah 34). The closing harvest scenes rework Joel 3:13 and Isaiah 63, and the Son of Man on the cloud is Daniel 7:13. Second Temple texts such as 1 Enoch 100, 4 Ezra 13 and 15 and 2 Baruch supply parallels to the Messiah on Zion and blood up to the horses' bridles.

The Greco-Roman background is just as present. 'Gospel' was imperial vocabulary for the good news of Augustus' birth and accession; hymn choirs sang the emperor's praises at provincial festivals; the kithara was Apollo's and Nero's instrument. Babylon as a code name for Rome appears in Jewish texts after the temple's destruction in 70, which some scholars take as support for a late date of Revelation, while preterists argue that the prophetic critique of faithless Jerusalem explains the image; Babylon's identity is disputed. The vivid harvest imagery would resonate in the grain and wine country of Asia Minor, and Josephus' account of the siege of Jerusalem (blood in the streets, mass crucifixions outside the walls) is often cited by preterists.
The Lamb standing on Mount Zion

Zion is where God installs his king (Psalm 2:6) and where deliverance is found in the day of the LORD (Joel 2:32; Obadiah 17, 21); the LORD will reign on Mount Zion (Isaiah 24:23; Micah 4:7). In 4 Ezra 13:35-40 the Messiah stands on Mount Zion and gathers a peaceful multitude after destroying the hostile nations. Hebrews 12:22 calls believers already come to the heavenly Mount Zion.

The scene answers chapter 13: in contrast to the beast and its marked worshippers, the Lamb stands (as in 5:6, alive though slain) with his protected people. Interpreters disagree whether Zion here is heavenly, earthly, or both, and whether the scene is present or future.
The heavenly Zion and new-covenant community, with the first-century Jewish-Christian remnant protected as Jerusalem falls (Chilton, Gentry).
The faithful church gathered around Christ during the age of papal apostasy, a vision of the true church set against the false (Barnes, Elliott).
Often the literal Mount Zion in Jerusalem at Christ's return, with the 144,000 Jewish believers of Revelation 7 entering the millennial kingdom; some futurists see it as heavenly (Walvoord, Thomas).
The heavenly Zion, where the church militant is already secure in Christ (Hebrews 12:22), anticipating final glory (Hendriksen, Beale).
144,000 who had His name and His Father's name written on their foreheads

The number repeats the sealed 144,000 from the twelve tribes (Revelation 7:4-8): 12 x 12 x 1,000, the full people of God organised like Israel's tribes and military census (Numbers 1). The names on the forehead recall the high priest's gold plate inscribed 'Holy to the LORD' worn on the forehead (Exodus 28:36-38) and Ezekiel 9:4's mark on the faithful; Revelation 3:12 and 22:4 promise God's name on the overcomer.
Slaves and devotees could bear a master's or god's name; in the Roman world, names inscribed on persons or property signified ownership.

These are God's sealed and protected people, bearing his name as the counterpart of the beast's mark. Whether they are the same as the 'great multitude' of 7:9 or a distinct group (often Jewish believers) is disputed.
The first-century Jewish-Christian remnant, firstfruits of the new Israel, preserved through the judgment on Jerusalem (Chilton, Gentry).
144,000 literal Jewish believers, 12,000 from each tribe, converted and protected during the tribulation (Walvoord, Thomas).
The whole church, the true Israel, complete and secure, the same as the countless multitude of 7:9 viewed from another angle (Hendriksen, Beale, Bauckham).
The faithful remnant of true believers throughout the era of papal apostasy (Barnes).
A sound like the roar of many waters, loud thunder, and harpists strumming their harps

God's voice and the glory of his presence sound like many waters in Ezekiel 1:24 and 43:2 (and the risen Christ's voice in Revelation 1:15); thunder accompanies theophany at Sinai (Exodus 19:16). Harps (kithara) were temple instruments of the Levitical musicians (1 Chronicles 25:1-6; Psalm 33:2; 150:3).

The kithara was Apollo's instrument and was played at Greek festivals and imperial celebrations; Nero famously performed on it in public contests (Suetonius, Nero 20-25), so heavenly harp music may stand in pointed contrast.
The heavenly liturgy is overwhelming in power yet musical and joyful. The sound combines God's majesty with the worship of the redeemed.
They sang a new song before the throne; no one could learn the song except the 144,000

A 'new song' celebrates a new act of divine deliverance or creation (Psalm 33:3; 40:3; 96:1; 98:1; 144:9; Isaiah 42:10). Moses and Israel sang after the Red Sea crossing (Exodus 15), echoed in the 'song of Moses and of the Lamb' (Revelation 15:3).
Hymn choirs (hymnodoi) in Asia sang praises at festivals of the imperial cult; Pergamum had an association of hymn-singers devoted to Augustus and Roma.
Only the redeemed can learn the song because only they have experienced redemption; it is the song of the new exodus in the Lamb (5:9-10).
These are the ones who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins

Israel's soldiers abstained from sexual relations during holy war (Deuteronomy 23:9-10; 1 Samuel 21:5; 2 Samuel 11:11), and the Qumran War Scroll (1QM 7:3-7) requires ritual purity in the eschatological army. Israel is called a virgin daughter (2 Kings 19:21; Jeremiah 18:13), and idolatry is pictured as adultery or prostitution (Hosea 1-3; Ezekiel 16 and 23). Paul presents the church as a pure virgin betrothed to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2).
Temple prostitution and sexual immorality at guild and cult banquets were linked with idolatry in early Christian polemic (Revelation 2:14, 20).

Most interpreters take it figuratively: the 144,000 are an army of the Lamb ritually pure for holy war, and spiritually faithful, refusing the 'immorality' of Babylon (14:8; 17:2). Because the language is male (not defiled with women), many see the holy-war image rather than a literal statement about gender or celibacy. A minority, ancient and modern, take it literally of celibate men.
Some futurists take it literally of men who remain celibate during the tribulation's distress; others read it as moral and spiritual purity (Walvoord, Thomas).
Spiritual chastity of the whole church, which refuses idolatrous compromise (Beale, Hendriksen).
The faithful first-century remnant who kept themselves from the spiritual adultery of apostate Jerusalem (Chilton).
They follow the Lamb wherever He goes
Discipleship language from the Gospels (Mark 8:34; John 10:4, 27); Israel followed God in the wilderness (Jeremiah 2:2).
They are disciples who follow Christ even to death, in contrast to the whole world that 'followed the beast' (13:3).
Redeemed from among men as firstfruits to God and to the Lamb

The first portion of the harvest belonged to God (Exodus 23:19; Leviticus 23:9-21, offered at the festival of Firstfruits and at Shavuot/Pentecost). Israel itself was 'holy to the LORD, the firstfruits of his harvest' (Jeremiah 2:3). The New Testament applies the image to Christ's resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:20), to early converts (Romans 16:5) and to believers (James 1:18).
Greek cities and individuals offered aparchai (first portions) to gods at temples, a widely understood act of consecration.

The 144,000 are dedicated wholly to God as a sacrificial offering. Interpreters debate whether 'firstfruits' implies a later, larger harvest (a first group among others) or simply means 'an offering set apart' (as in Jeremiah 2:3).
The first generation of Jewish believers before AD 70, the firstfruits of the gospel's worldwide harvest (Chilton, Gentry).
Jewish converts in the tribulation, first of the great harvest that enters the millennium (Walvoord).
The whole church as God's consecrated offering, not a preliminary group (Beale, Hendriksen).
No lie was found in their mouths; they are blameless

Zephaniah 3:13 describes the remnant of Israel as speaking no lies, with no deceitful tongue; the Servant had no deceit in his mouth (Isaiah 53:9). 'Blameless' (amomos) is the Septuagint word for unblemished sacrificial animals (Leviticus 1:3; Numbers 6:14).
Their truthfulness contrasts with the 'lie' of the beast and false prophet (compare 21:27; 22:15, and 'the lie' of 2 Thessalonians 2:11); 'blameless' continues the sacrificial picture of firstfruits.
Another angel flying overhead, with the eternal gospel to proclaim to every nation, tribe, tongue and people

The angel 'in midheaven' (mesouranema, the zenith where all can hear) matches the eagle of 8:13. Psalm 96:2-3, 10 calls for declaring God's salvation and glory among the nations and announces that he comes to judge; Isaiah 52:7 announces good news of God's reign. Jesus said the gospel must be preached to all nations before the end (Mark 13:10).

Euangelion ('good news') was imperial vocabulary: the Priene calendar inscription (9 BC) hails the birthday of Augustus as the beginning of 'good tidings' for the world. John's 'eternal' gospel outlasts any imperial proclamation.

A final call to repentance and worship of the Creator before judgment, addressed to every people. Whether it is the Christian gospel itself or a last-hour summons to acknowledge God (as 14:7 suggests) is debated.

Successive proclamations in church history: the Reformation's recovery of the gospel and the modern missionary movement; Seventh-day Adventists identify the three angels with the advent message from the 1840s (Elliott, Barnes, Smith).
A literal angelic proclamation during the tribulation, a last offer of grace before final judgment (Walvoord, Thomas).
The worldwide preaching of the gospel in the apostolic generation before the judgment of AD 70 (Colossians 1:23; Matthew 24:14) (Chilton).
The church's ongoing mission summoning all nations to worship God as Creator and Judge (Hendriksen, Beale).
Fear God and give Him glory, because the hour of His judgment has come; worship the One who made the heavens and the earth and the sea and the springs of waters

Echoes the fourth commandment's grounding of the Sabbath in creation (Exodus 20:11) and Psalm 146:6. 'Fear God and give him glory' is the language of conversion (Jeremiah 13:16; Revelation 11:13). Paul's appeal to pagans at Lystra uses the same creator formula (Acts 14:15).
Polytheistic Asia worshipped deities of sky, earth, sea and springs (river gods, nymphs and healing springs at sanctuaries such as Hierapolis); worshipping the one Creator dethrones them all.

The fourfold creation list (heaven, earth, sea, springs) corresponds to the realms struck by the first four trumpets and bowls, so the Creator is also the Judge. The 'hour' of judgment signals imminence.
Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, who made all the nations drink the wine of the passion of her immorality

Isaiah 21:9 cries 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon'; Jeremiah 51:7-8 calls Babylon a golden cup that made the nations drunk, and announces her sudden fall; Nebuchadnezzar boasts of 'Babylon the great' (Daniel 4:30). After AD 70 Jewish writers used 'Babylon' as a code name for Rome, the new destroyer of the temple (4 Ezra 3:1-2, 28-31; 2 Baruch 11:1; Sibylline Oracles 5.143, 159), as 1 Peter 5:13 probably does.

Rome was the commercial and political hub of the Mediterranean, enriched by provincial trade (Revelation 18). Some scholars argue that the Babylon code arose because Rome, like Babylon, destroyed Jerusalem, which they take as evidence for a post-70 date; preterists answer that the prophetic tradition of faithless Jerusalem as harlot (Isaiah 1:21; Ezekiel 16) explains the image without that assumption. The identity of Babylon is disputed.

This first mention of Babylon anticipates chapters 17-18. The prophetic past tense ('fallen') announces her doom as certain. 'Wine of passion' (thymos can mean both passion and wrath) links her seduction of the nations with the wrath it brings.
Many partial preterists (Gentry, Chilton) identify Babylon as apostate Jerusalem, the city 'where their Lord was crucified' (11:8), judged in AD 70; others in the same camp identify her with Rome.
Papal Rome, the apostate church allied with political power; Protestant confessional traditions long read it this way (Barnes, Elliott, Smith).
An end-time world system centred either on a revived Rome (Walvoord) or on a literally rebuilt city of Babylon in Iraq (some dispensationalists, e.g. Charles Dyer); futurists differ among themselves.
The seductive world-system of economic, political and cultural idolatry in every age, embodied first in Rome (Hendriksen, Beale).
First-century Rome as a type of every proud, oppressive culture that will be finally judged (Bauckham, Osborne).
He too will drink the wine of God's anger, poured undiluted into the cup of His wrath

The cup of God's wrath is a prophetic image for judgment (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17, 22; Jeremiah 25:15-29; Habakkuk 2:16). Jesus spoke of drinking the cup in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). The word-play is exact: those who drank Babylon's wine (14:8) must drink God's.

Greeks and Romans normally mixed wine with water; drinking it unmixed (akratos) was a mark of barbarism or excess. 'Mixed unmixed' (kekerasmenou akratou) is a vivid paradox: the cup is fully prepared, with nothing diluting its strength.
Judgment corresponds to sin: those who share Babylon's intoxicating idolatry receive God's full, undiluted wrath.
Tormented in fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and of the Lamb; the smoke of their torment rises forever and ever; no rest day and night

Fire and sulfur rained on Sodom, whose smoke rose like a furnace (Genesis 19:24, 28); Isaiah 34:9-10 says Edom's smoke will go up forever and never be quenched, language of permanent desolation. 1 Enoch 48:9 pictures the wicked burning before the righteous; Isaiah 66:24 ends with the corpses of rebels seen by the faithful. 'No rest day and night' inverts the unceasing worship of the living creatures (4:8).
Sulfur (theion) was associated with divine judgment and with volcanic regions; Asia Minor's volcanic and hot-spring landscapes made the images familiar.

This is one of the Bible's most solemn warnings of final judgment, aimed at deterring believers from worshipping the beast. Interpreters agree it is a warning of real and final divine judgment; they disagree on the nature of that judgment. The traditional view across all hermeneutical schools is eternal conscious punishment; some evangelicals (conditional immortality or annihilationism) argue the 'smoke rising forever' is an Old Testament idiom for irreversible destruction (Isaiah 34:10), a view traditionalists answer by pointing to 'no rest day and night' and 20:10.
Preterists see Sodom-and-Edom imagery applied first to a historical judgment (on Jerusalem or Rome) while also affirming final eternal judgment (Chilton, Gentry).
The eternal punishment of those who take the mark in the tribulation, i.e. the lake of fire (Walvoord, Thomas).
The final, irreversible judgment of all who give their allegiance to the world-system rather than God (Hendriksen, Beale).
Here is a call for the perseverance of the saints who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus
Repeats 13:10 and 12:17. Keeping God's commandments recalls the covenant at Sinai; the faith of (or in) Jesus stresses loyalty to Christ. Daniel 12:12 blesses those who endure.
The warnings of 14:9-11 serve pastoral exhortation: believers must endure rather than compromise. Whether 'faith of Jesus' means faith in Jesus or faithfulness like his is debated grammatically.
Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from this moment on; they will rest from their labors, for their deeds will follow them

The second of seven beatitudes in Revelation. Rest for the righteous dead appears in Isaiah 57:1-2 and Daniel 12:13; Hebrews 4 develops the Sabbath rest of God's people. 4 Ezra 7:35 and 2 Baruch 14:12 speak of works or righteous deeds accompanying the righteous. A later rabbinic saying (Pirqe Avot 6:9) says that at death neither silver nor gold accompanies a person, only Torah and good deeds.
Greco-Roman epitaphs often expressed resignation or hopelessness about death ('I was not, I was, I am not, I do not care'); John promises blessing and rest.
Martyrs and all who die faithful are blessed: their toil ends and their faithful works are remembered by God. 'From now on' (ap' arti) marks the present era of persecution.
A special comfort to believers dying in the coming Neronic and Jewish War crises, and to all believers thereafter (Gentry).
Especially the martyrs of the tribulation (Walvoord).
All believers who die faithful in any age (Hendriksen).
One like the Son of Man seated on a white cloud, with a golden crown on His head and a sharp sickle in His hand

Daniel 7:13-14: one like a son of man comes with the clouds to receive everlasting dominion. Jesus applied this to himself (Mark 14:62; Matthew 24:30). Clouds are the vehicle of divine presence and judgment (Exodus 13:21; Psalm 104:3; Isaiah 19:1). Joel 3:13 commands, 'Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe.'
The golden crown (stephanos) was the victor's wreath and the triumphing general's crown; Roman emperors wore golden wreaths in triumphs.

Most identify the figure as Christ, the victorious Son of Man (compare 1:13). A minority argue that he is an angel because he receives instruction from 'another angel' (14:15); responders note that the angel merely relays God's timing, as Christ himself said only the Father knows the hour (Mark 13:32).
Christ coming in judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70 (Matthew 24:30; 26:64) and gathering his elect (Chilton, Gentry).
Christ's final judgment at the end of the historical sequence the book has traced (Barnes).
Christ's second coming at the end of the tribulation (Walvoord, Thomas).
Christ's final coming in judgment at the end of history (Hendriksen, Beale).
Swing Your sickle and reap, for the crop of the earth is ripe; the earth was harvested

Joel 3:13 pairs grain harvest and winepress as judgment on the nations in the valley of decision. Jesus uses harvest for the gathering of the righteous at the end of the age (Matthew 13:30, 39-43; Mark 4:29; John 4:35-38). Grain harvest in Israel (barley, wheat) came in spring and early summer, celebrated at Passover/Firstfruits and Pentecost.
Harvest was the economic heart of agrarian Asia Minor; reaping with sickles was a universal image of death (later the Grim Reaper).

Commentators divide on whether the grain harvest (14:14-16) is the ingathering of the righteous, followed by the vintage of judgment (14:17-20), or whether both are judgment as in Joel 3:13. Since the term 'firstfruits' was just used of believers, many see a positive harvest of the saints; others note the 'dried up' or 'ripe' (xeraino) language suggests judgment.
The gathering of the elect through the gospel and the judgment on Israel at the end of the old-covenant age (Chilton).
Separating the righteous and wicked at Christ's return; many dispensationalists read both harvests as judgments at Armageddon (Walvoord).
The final gathering of God's people at the last judgment, paired with the judgment of the wicked (Beale, Bauckham).
Another angel came out of the temple; still another, with authority over the fire, came from the altar

The altar in Revelation is where the souls of martyrs cry out for justice (6:9-11) and where the incense of the saints' prayers rises before fire is thrown on the earth (8:3-5). The perpetual fire of the altar (Leviticus 6:12-13) and coals from the altar used in judgment (Ezekiel 10:2) lie behind 'authority over the fire'.

The vintage of judgment comes from the heavenly temple and altar, so it is God's answer to the martyrs' prayers. Jewish tradition assigned angels to elements (1 Enoch 60:11-21; Jubilees 2:2), and Revelation has angels of the winds (7:1) and waters (16:5).
Gather the clusters of grapes from the vine of the earth, because its grapes are ripe

Israel is God's vine or vineyard (Isaiah 5:1-7; Psalm 80:8-16; Jeremiah 2:21; Hosea 10:1), and Jesus is the true vine (John 15). The 'vine of Sodom' (Deuteronomy 32:32-33) produces poisonous grapes. Joel 3:13 calls for treading the full winepress of the nations.

Grape harvest (vintage) came in late summer and autumn and was celebrated with festivals of Dionysus in the Greek world; Asia Minor's valleys were famous wine country. In Judaism the autumn vintage coincided with the festival of Tabernacles (ingathering).
The 'vine of the earth' (or 'of the land') stands in contrast to the true vine: it is humanity organised in rebellion and ripe for judgment.
The 'vine of the land': apostate Israel, the vineyard that produced bad fruit (Isaiah 5), judged in AD 70 (Chilton).
The ungodly nations gathered against Christ at Armageddon (Walvoord).
Unbelieving humanity in rebellion, ripe for final judgment (Beale, Hendriksen).
The great winepress of God's wrath was trodden outside the city

Isaiah 63:1-6 pictures the LORD returning from Edom with garments stained red from treading the winepress of the nations alone; Lamentations 1:15 says the Lord trod Judah like grapes in a winepress; Joel 3:2, 12-14 places the nations' judgment in the Valley of Jehoshaphat, traditionally the Kidron valley outside Jerusalem; Zechariah 14:2-4 has the nations gathered against Jerusalem. Executions took place outside the camp or city (Leviticus 24:14; Numbers 15:35), as did Jesus' crucifixion (Hebrews 13:12).

Ancient winepresses were stone vats where grapes were trodden by foot, the juice flowing down a channel; red juice splashing on clothes made the image of blood vivid. Roman sieges ended with mass slaughter outside the walls: Josephus describes the crucifixion of thousands of captives outside Jerusalem during the siege (Jewish War 5.446-451).

God's judgment of rebellious humanity is complete and terrible. Revelation 19:15 shows Christ treading this winepress. 'The city' is probably Jerusalem or the holy city (the beloved city of 20:9), i.e. God's people are protected inside while judgment falls outside; others see it as Babylon.
The destruction of the Jewish nation in AD 70, with slaughter around Jerusalem and throughout the land (Chilton, Gentry).
